connection: The solution and ScratchPad experiments exist, but Domain still contains only the class-library template. This is the first session that adds TimeClock business code. Create the first production domain models—Address, Employee, and ClockEntry—from the verified product vocabulary.
objectives: Distinguish a class definition from an object instance.
Use a constructor to establish required state.
Read properties as named parts of an object's public state.
Implement ClockIn end to end: construct a ClockEntry and persist it through a repository.

visuals.title: A class defines a shape
visuals.explanation: Employee and ClockEntry describe available construction, state, and behavior; each new expression creates a distinct instance.

visuals.title: Construction establishes required state
visuals.explanation: ClockEntry's constructor takes only employeeId and clockIn -- there is no ClockOut parameter, because a freshly created entry is always open.

visuals.title: Properties expose named state
visuals.explanation: EmployeeId, ClockIn, and ClockOut let callers read meaningful state; ClockOut has a private setter so only ClockOutEmployee can change it.

visuals.title: Instances keep independent values
visuals.explanation: Two ClockEntry objects follow the same class definition but hold different employee ids and timestamps.

preQuiz.prompt: What does new ClockEntry(employeeId, DateTime.Now) produce?
options: A ClockEntry object reference with ClockOut left null
preQuiz.explanation: new invokes the constructor; the real constructor only sets EmployeeId and ClockIn, so ClockOut stays null (open).

preQuiz.prompt: Why does the real ClockEntry constructor have no ClockOut parameter?
options: A newly created entry is always open, and only ClockOutEmployee is allowed to close it later
ClockOut is not a real property
preQuiz.explanation: Clock In only ever needs who and when; the domain expresses "currently on the clock" as ClockOut being null, not as a placeholder value.

preQuiz.prompt: If two ClockEntry objects exist for the same employee on different days, does changing one change the other?
preQuiz.explanation: They are separate instances with independent property values.

concept.title: Classes define; objects exist
paragraphs: ClockEntry is a class: a reusable definition. entry is a variable whose value refers to one ClockEntry object.
Keeping that vocabulary precise prevents confusion between changing a definition and creating an instance.

concept.title: Constructors establish invariants
paragraphs: The real ClockEntry constructor does no validation at all -- it simply assigns EmployeeId and ClockIn. The invariant it protects is structural, not a range check: there is no way to construct an entry that already has a ClockOut value, because the constructor never accepts one.
This is a deliberate, minimal design. Compare it with Employee's constructor, which is equally simple: it assigns EmployeeId, Name, and Address with no validation either.

concept.title: Properties communicate intent
paragraphs: EmployeeId and ClockIn are get-only: the constructor establishes them, callers may read them, and ordinary code cannot assign new values later. Name and Address use get and set because this model currently permits those values to change.
Session 06 stops at the state known during clock-in. ClockOut, a private setter, and completion rules arrive in Session 07, where their purpose can be explained instead of copied prematurely.

This course intentionally uses the original application's minimal Address shape: Street and City. A production postal address might also require state or region, postal code, and country, but those values are outside the current verified requirements and are not added speculatively.

concept.title: The Domain project owns the business models
paragraphs: Address, Employee, and ClockEntry belong inside the PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain project because they describe the business. In VS Code, that project appears as the src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain folder. The folder path tells you where to create the files; the .csproj file defines which project owns and compiles them.

The App project needs a ProjectReference to Domain before Session06ModelDemo can consume Address, Employee, or ClockEntry. In the lab, add that reference explicitly, then inspect the App project file so you can connect the command with the ProjectReference it creates.

review: The lab uses production because that is the most natural environment for this concept.
Every referenced application artifact was created in this session or an earlier session.
Earlier production code, tests, and ScratchPad experiments remain intact.

postQuiz.prompt: Why does ClockEntryService.ClockIn call SaveClockEntry immediately after construction?
options: A constructed-but-unsaved ClockEntry has no observable effect on the rest of the app
Save is required by the C# language
postQuiz.explanation: The repository's in-memory list is the only place other code can find the entry later; skipping Save makes the method look complete while doing nothing observable.

postQuiz.prompt: What would happen if ClockOut had a public setter instead of a private one?
options: Any code anywhere could set ClockOut directly, bypassing ClockOutEmployee's "can only clock out once" check
Nothing -- private and public setters behave identically
The class would fail to compile
postQuiz.explanation: A private setter keeps the only legal way to close an entry inside ClockOutEmployee, which is exactly the guard Session 24 exercises.

postQuiz.prompt: What do the ClockEntry constructor's two parameters establish?
options: Which employee and when they started -- nothing else, because nothing else is knowable yet
postQuiz.explanation: Clock In only ever needs who and when; there is nothing else to construct with at that point in time.

reflections: Why does the real ClockEntry constructor accept no ClockOut parameter at all, rather than one that defaults to null?
What would break elsewhere in the domain if ClockIn defaulted to DateTime.MinValue instead of always requiring DateTime.Now?
How is an object different from the variable that refers to it?
whatBreaks: Removing the private setter on ClockOut lets any code close an entry without going through ClockOutEmployee's guard, silently breaking the "can only clock out once" invariant Session 24 tests. Removing SaveClockEntry from ClockIn makes the method compile and run with no observable effect. Removing constructor assignment for EmployeeId or ClockIn breaks the non-null guarantee those properties depend on.
summary: A class defines construction, state, and behavior. ClockEntry's constructor establishes only what Clock In can know at that moment -- who and when -- and leaves ClockOut null on purpose; ClockEntryService.ClockIn constructs, then saves, completing the real substeps from Step 42 of the source project.
